analysis.title: Key market themes Q4 2026
key_insights: Energy shock: central banks that first looked through the spring energy spike have lost patience as prices rose again over the summer. Short-term inflation expectations track oil closely, and US pricing has moved from about three cuts to about 2.5 hikes by year-end. SEB calls this repricing the single most important driver of the rise in global yields.

SEB does not expect energy prices to fall meaningfully before the US midterms on 3 November, because it sees Iran as having little incentive to ease pressure before the election. European gas prices are at their highest since 2022 and inventories are seasonally low.

Global growth has been more resilient than expected. Manufacturing has held up on an investment boom led by AI, defence, green investment and infrastructure, while services PMI mostly moved sideways. Both manufacturing and services PMIs rose strongly in September, which may mean the investment boom is spilling into the wider economy. Higher energy prices and rates remain the main downside risks.

US midterms: Democrats are increasingly likely to win the House and the Senate is becoming more competitive. A Democratic Congress would limit Trump's new fiscal reforms, while he keeps control over trade and foreign policy and can veto legislation. A Democratic Senate could block appointments, including to the Fed and Supreme Court. Gridlock raises budget and debt-ceiling risk, though fiscal policy could turn somewhat more expansionary if social spending is traded for defence spending.

Public finances: rising bond yields are pressuring heavily indebted France and the US. Both run deficits of about 5-6% of GDP, but the US has much stronger growth. SEB expects no meaningful French deficit reduction over the next year and sees a risk of further deterioration.

French risk premia have risen sharply. French swap spreads are widening while other G10 spreads are stable. The France-Germany 10Y spread is at its highest since 2012 and France pays the highest sovereign yield in the euro area.

European politics: France holds a presidential election in April 2027 with public finances central to the debate, including unconventional proposals such as writing off French debt. The election could trigger a snap parliamentary election. AfD has gained momentum in Germany with several state elections in 2027, and Italy and others point to stronger right-wing forces. The trend is toward political fragmentation and more EU- and euro-sceptic policy.

Japan: the recent yen intervention was the largest ever and the US took part for the first time in 30 years. Japan sells dollars and buys yen, drawing down reserves largely held in US Treasuries. Washington wants a stronger yen but does not want Japan selling Treasuries while US yields are high, hence US verbal intervention.

A more hawkish BoJ could narrow the Japan-US rate gap, cut carry incentives and reduce the need for more intervention, though US rates also need to fall. Further intervention could push up long-end US yields, and a shift by investors such as GPIF toward domestic assets could affect global bond and equity markets.

China: its global trade surplus keeps reaching new highs despite a sharp drop in its surplus with the US, and a growing share is redirected to Europe. This raises pressure on European industry and the odds of more EU trade barriers. China shows few signs of changing its subsidy-driven capacity buildup, so EU-China tension is a risk while transatlantic trade relations are already strained.

Fed under Kevin Warsh: he first sounded relatively dovish but has shifted clearly hawkish. So far he has aligned with the internal Fed consensus and resisted political pressure for faster cuts. He is critical of forward guidance, favours less predictable communication and wants a narrower, clearer policy mandate.

Warsh has set up five task forces on communications, the balance sheet, data, productivity and jobs (how AI is changing the economy), and inflation frameworks. These could reshape the Fed's reaction function and how policy is conducted.

Treasury: Secretary Scott Bessent is the most interventionist in decades, taking part in efforts to support the yen and contain US yields. Treasury has announced larger buybacks of long-dated Treasuries with room to increase them. Volumes are small, but many see it as an early 'Treasury Operation Twist' to flatten the curve.
Further attempts to push down long-term yields could revive the USD debasement theme, meaning a weaker dollar and concern about lost US purchasing power.

AI: hyperscaler free cash flow has fallen sharply as investment accelerated, and some companies increasingly rely on banks and capital markets for financing. Several AI companies have postponed IPOs, which limits transparency into their financials. Investor concern is shifting from valuations toward leverage, financing needs and sustainability, and a correction in AI assets could reach the broader economic cycle.

risk_factors: Energy prices staying high through the midterms, keeping inflation expectations and policy rates higher
Higher energy prices and interest rates weighing on growth despite recent resilience
Fiscal gridlock and budget or debt-ceiling fights after the US midterms
French fiscal deterioration and political risk ahead of the April 2027 presidential election
Further Japanese intervention pushing up long-end US yields, or GPIF shifting toward domestic assets
Rising EU-China trade tension from China's export surplus
Treasury efforts to cap long-term yields reviving the USD debasement theme
A correction in leveraged AI-related assets spreading beyond equities to the real economy
geopolitical: US midterm elections on 3 November, with Democrats increasingly likely to regain the House and the Senate becoming more competitive
Iran seen as having little incentive to ease energy-market pressure before the US midterms
French presidential election in April 2027, with a possible snap parliamentary election and unconventional debt proposals such as writing off French debt
AfD momentum in Germany ahead of several 2027 state elections, and stronger right-wing forces in Italy and elsewhere in Europe
Largest-ever Japanese yen intervention, with the US participating for the first time in 30 years
China's rising trade surplus redirected toward Europe, raising the odds of EU trade barriers and EU-China tension
Trump's repeated demands for lower rates and pressure on the Fed under Warsh

tension_points.bull_case: Manufacturing has stayed resilient on an AI, defence, green and infrastructure investment boom, and September manufacturing and services PMIs both picked up strongly, which could mean a broader recovery.
tension_points.bear_case: Services activity has been subdued and higher energy prices and interest rates remain important downside risks.

tension_points.bull_case: AI-related investment is increasingly important for the real US and global economy and supports the wider investment boom.
tension_points.bear_case: Hyperscaler free cash flow has fallen sharply, financing needs are growing, several AI IPOs were postponed, and a correction could affect the broader economic cycle.

theme_stances.key_argument: Rising energy prices pushed up inflation expectations, forcing central banks to turn hawkish and lifting global yields.
theme_stances.evidence: central banks have lost patience and need to respond to higher inflation expectations

theme_stances.key_argument: France is unlikely to reduce its deficit meaningfully over the next year, and its risk premia are widening ahead of the 2027 election.
theme_stances.evidence: French risk premia have risen sharply

theme_stances.key_argument: Falling hyperscaler free cash flow and reliance on outside financing shift the concern from valuations to leverage.
theme_stances.evidence: Investor concerns are increasingly shifting from high valuations towards leverage
